quote: the seven stars of heaven's highest realm
note: The seven golden candlesticks that led the procession in Canto 29, usually read as the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Dante calls them the Septentrion, the name of the seven stars of the Bear, and says they belong to the highest heaven, the Empyrean, where God is.

Dante's Italian says "the lower one": the seven stars of the Bear in our own sky, near the pole, which sailors steered by. The lights of the procession guide the soul as those stars guide a helmsman to port.
The twenty-four elders who walked behind the candlesticks in Canto 29, crowned with lilies. They stand for the books of the Old Testament.

context: It has halted with the chariot it draws, and the whole procession turns to face it.

note: The two-wheeled triumphal chariot at the center of the procession, usually read as the Church. Everything in the pageant has been leading up to the one who will appear on it.
The elder who stands for the Song of Songs, the Bible's love poem, traditionally written by Solomon. He sings a verse from his own book.
Song of Songs 4:8, sung in Latin in Dante's text: "Veni, sponsa, de Libano". Medieval readers took the bride of that poem as the Church or the soul loved by God. Here the call summons Beatrice.
The Last Judgment, when the dead will rise and take up their bodies again. The angels spring up on the chariot as suddenly as that.

quote: a hundred rose at the elder's voice
note: A hundred angels. Dante puts the phrase "at the voice of so great an elder" in Latin, as if it too came from scripture, but it is his own.

The crowd's greeting to Christ as he rode into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:9), given in Latin: "Benedictus qui venis". The angels keep the masculine "he" though they are welcoming Beatrice. She arrives as Christ will arrive at the end of time, to judge.

A line of Virgil's, quoted in his Latin: "Manibus o date lilia plenis". In Aeneid 6 it mourns Marcellus, the heir of Augustus who died young. Set beside a verse of the Gospel, it becomes a welcome, and a last honor to Virgil moments before he is gone.

context: Her first appearance in person. She died in 1290, ten years before the journey, and it was she who sent Virgil to rescue Dante (Inferno 2). She is still veiled, and Dante knows her before he can see her face.

note: White veil, green mantle, flame-red dress: the colors of faith, hope and love, the three theological virtues. In the Vita Nuova, Dante's early book about her, Beatrice is dressed in red the first time he sees her.

quote: before I'd grown beyond my boyhood
note: In the Vita Nuova Dante says he first saw Beatrice when he was nearly nine and she was eight, and that love ruled him from that day.

quote: I know the marks of the ancient flame
note: A translation of Dido's words in Aeneid 4, when she feels herself falling in love with Aeneas: "agnosco veteris vestigia flammae". Dante's last words to Virgil are Virgil's own line.

context: He has gone without a word, back to Limbo. His last speech was at the end of Canto 27, where he crowned Dante master of himself. His name comes three times in three lines, often heard as an echo of Virgil's own Orpheus calling three times for the lost Eurydice.
All the beauty of Eden, which Eve lost for humankind, is around Dante, and it cannot keep him from weeping for Virgil.

note: Dante's Italian says his cheeks had been cleansed with dew. At the foot of the mountain Virgil washed the grime and tears of Hell from Dante's face with dew (Purgatorio 1). The face Virgil cleaned is stained again by tears for Virgil.

The only time Dante's name appears in the whole poem, and it is Beatrice's first word to him. He apologizes for recording it a few lines on: medieval writers held it bad manners to name oneself without need.
A deeper wound than the loss of Virgil: the account she is about to demand of his own sins.
Not the gentle reunion a reader expects. Beatrice's first likeness is to a commander inspecting his fleet, and she speaks as a judge before she speaks as the woman he loved.

context: Dante is still on the near bank. The procession, the chariot and Beatrice are on the other side, and he cannot cross until he has confessed.

note: The olive, sacred to Minerva, the Roman goddess of wisdom. The olive is also a sign of peace.
The Italian hammers on one word: "Ben son, ben son Beatrice", roughly "I am, I truly am Beatrice". It is the only time in the poem she speaks her own name.
Dante's verb means "deign": how did you condescend to come here at last? Usually read as bitter irony, aimed at a man who for years thought he had better things to pursue.

context: The happiness humankind was made for is here, and Dante went looking for it everywhere else.

note: The stream of Lethe at his feet. It shows him his own shamed face, and he cannot bear to look at it.

quote: In you, Lord, I have hoped
note: Psalm 31 (30 in the Latin Bible), a psalm of trust in God's mercy. The angels sing its first eight verses and stop at "you have set my feet in a wide place", before the psalm turns to lament. They are pleading for Dante.
The Apennines, the mountain spine of Italy. Dante's phrase is "the living beams": the trees on the ridge, which will one day be timber, with the snow frozen among them.
The cold north-east winds that blow into Italy across the Adriatic from the Slavic lands.
Africa. In the tropics the sun at certain times stands straight overhead at noon and bodies cast no shadow. The warm south wind from there melts the snow, as the angels' pity melts Dante.
The turning heavens, which were believed to make music as they moved. The angels sing in tune with it.
The angels see everything in God, so nothing that happens in time is hidden from them. They need no explanation. Beatrice answers them aloud so that Dante will hear the charge against him.

The heavenly spheres. Medieval science held that the stars and planets shape a person's gifts at birth. Dante was born under Gemini, and in Paradiso 22 he thanks those stars for his talent. Grace, she adds, gave him even more.
The Italian is "vita nova", new or young life. It is also the title of the book Dante wrote in the early 1290s about his love for Beatrice, the Vita Nuova.

quote: the threshold of my second age
note: Beatrice died in June 1290, aged twenty-four. Dante divided life into ages, the first ending at twenty-five, so she died just as she was about to enter the second.

The Italian word can mean "others" or "another". Readers have long argued over what is meant: another woman, such as the lady who comforts Dante at the end of the Vita Nuova; the study of philosophy, which he later said that lady stood for; or worldly aims in general. Dante does not say.
The Vita Nuova tells of visions of Beatrice that came to Dante after her death and turned him back to her for a time.

quote: to show him the lost souls
note: The journey through Hell. The whole of the Inferno was Beatrice's last resort, when nothing gentler had worked.
Limbo, in Hell. Beatrice left Heaven and went down there to ask Virgil to rescue Dante, and she wept as she asked (Inferno 2).

quote: penitence that flows forth in tears
note: This canto and the next follow the steps of the sacrament of penance: sorrow for sin, confession in one's own words, then making amends. Only after that may Dante drink the water that wipes out the memory of sin.
